name: Bandwagon Effect
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Everyone Else Is Buying It: The Bandwagon Effect and Blockchain Hype Cycles
lesson.summary: The bandwagon effect is the tendency to adopt a belief or behavior because many other people have adopted it, turning rising participation itself, rather than any underlying evidence, into the main reason people pile into a blockchain asset or project.
lesson.body:
The bandwagon effect describes the tendency for a person to adopt a belief, join a trend, or take an action simply because they observe that many other people are already doing it, treating the size of the crowd as evidence in its own right rather than as an incidental fact about popularity. Unlike confirmation bias, which filters information to protect a belief someone already holds, the bandwagon effect can create the belief in the first place: a person with no strong prior opinion about a token or protocol can be moved toward buying it purely by observing rising prices, growing social media mentions, or friends and coworkers discussing it, independent of any technical evaluation.

Blockchain markets amplify the bandwagon effect through visible, real time signals of crowd participation that most traditional assets lack: a token's price chart, its trading volume, its holder count, and its trending status on social platforms are all public, constantly updating, and easy to interpret as everyone is doing this, so it must be worth doing. The 2017 initial coin offering boom and the 2021 NFT boom both show the pattern clearly: participation accelerated fastest not when the strongest technical arguments for a given project appeared, but when visible signals, rapidly rising floor prices, a rush of new wallets, prominent figures publicly buying in, made joining feel like the default, unremarkable choice rather than a risk requiring independent justification.

The bandwagon effect and confirmation bias reinforce each other in a way worth naming explicitly, because together they explain why blockchain hype cycles can be so hard to interrupt from inside the community experiencing one. The bandwagon effect pulls a new participant in based on visible crowd size; confirmation bias then keeps that participant filtering incoming information to protect the decision they just made, seeking out the community's continued growth as further confirmation, and dismissing warnings as coming from people who, in the community's own framing, simply do not get it. Each bias supplies fuel the other one burns, and the resulting cycle can run for a long time on social proof alone, well past the point where the underlying fundamentals would justify the participation on their own.

The bandwagon effect also shaped the contentious hard forks covered earlier, though in a subtler way: once a faction of a blockchain community commits publicly to one side of a fork, visible momentum, more developers, more exchanges listing the new chain, more public endorsements, becomes a self reinforcing signal that pulls undecided participants toward whichever side already looks larger, independent of the technical merits of the tradeoff that caused the split in the first place. Recognizing the bandwagon effect for what it is, a feature of crowd psychology rather than a signal about underlying value or correctness, is one of the more durable habits a skeptic of any hype driven market can build.
